claims.text: A controlled heat treatment can induce a moderate degree of short-range atomic order in a high-entropy alloy.
Moderate short-range atomic order creates local variations in stacking-fault energy.
Moderate short-range order enhances dislocation mobility.
Nanoscale twinning provides an additional deformation mode that helps retain toughness.
Nanoscale twinning and adaptive dislocation slip deflect cracks and dissipate energy.
Excessively severe heat treatment causes brittle intergranular precipitates to form.
Excessive heat treatment can over-homogenize the alloy and remove beneficial local stacking-fault-energy variations.
Brittle phases or removal of local stacking-fault-energy variations impair toughness.
The baseline is a solution-treated, single-phase homogeneous alloy with low short-range order and no significant brittle precipitates.
Annealing below and above a critical temperature can modulate short-range order without causing phase segregation.
All processing parameters other than annealing temperature are to be held constant, with testing under quasi-static loading at ambient to moderate temperatures.
An optimized heat treatment will produce greater fracture toughness than the solution-treated baseline.
The optimized heat treatment will increase impact-energy absorption and delay crack initiation.
The optimized heat treatment will produce a higher density of nanoscale twins than the baseline.
Treatment above the optimal temperature will markedly reduce toughness and will be accompanied by brittle intergranular precipitates.
The proposed behavior is limited primarily to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys under conditions avoiding severe segregation and macroscopic phase transformations.
The critical annealing temperature and duration depend on alloy composition and processing history.

contradictions.description: The intervention is specified to modulate short-range order without triggering phase segregation, but the high-temperature branch predicts formation of brittle intergranular precipitates, which entails secondary-phase segregation.

The stated validity boundary excludes severe segregation and macroscopic phase transformations, while the predicted and falsifying high-temperature behavior requires brittle precipitate formation. It is not clarified whether nanoscale precipitation remains inside the boundary.
